TAMKEEN • POLICY & STRATEGY
A DECADE IN
THE RANKINGS
Key trends, and the biggest risers and fallers, in the QS and Times Higher Education World University Rankings over the past decade
DECEMBER 2026
 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
 

 

Asia's share of Top 100 in the World University Rankings more than doubled, driven by Greater China
■Asia's share of the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings (WUR) Top 100 grew from 9% in 2016 to 21% in 2027.

 

■China's number of THE WUR Top 100 universities grew from 2 in 2016 to 8 in 2027, followed by Hong Kong (2 to 5) and South Korea (1 to 4). Each rise lines up with sustained public funding: China's Double First-Class programme, which funds about 140 universities, government funding allocated through Hong Kong's University Grants Committee, and Korea's Brain Korea 21 programme.

 

US is losing ground, especially below the Top 100
■The US's WUR Top 100 university count fell: 39 to 37 on THE. However, top universities (Harvard, MIT and Stanford) hold almost the same rank as a decade ago.
■In the WUR Top 500, the drop is noticeable: the US lost 26 institutions on THE, the largest net decline of any country this decade (see chart).

 

The Gulf is a second growth engine, after China
■Saudi Arabia (+8 institutions) is the next-biggest gainer in the WUR Top 500 after China, and the UAE (+6 institutions) is close behind.
■Khalifa University's QS rank climbed 258 places this decade, up to rank 147 in 2027. That's the largest gain of any UAE university. The climb followed a 2017 merger that brought Khalifa University, the Petroleum Institute and the Masdar Institute together into one flagship.
■Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 set a clear goal: at least five institutions in the global Top 200 by 2030. King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals became the first Arab university to break into the QS Top 100, and now sits at rank 63.
■Qatar's Hamad Bin Khalifa University, which debuted on THE in 2027 at rank 126, is currently the highest-ranked Gulf university on THE.

 

 

 
THE GLOBAL LANDSCAPE
 

 

The decade's key shifts: China, the Gulf (Saudi Arabia and UAE) and the US

 

01
Four of the decade's biggest shifts came from China, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which grew, and the US, which declined. Malaysia, France, the UK and Italy also moved substantially.
China added 25 universities to THE's Top 500 over the decade and quadrupled its Top 100 count, from 2 to 8. The rise lines up with the Double First-Class programme.
—Double First-Class funds about 140 universities to build world-class research capacity, in five-year cycles, since 2016.
—Funding is paired with strong accountability mechanisms: after the first cycle, the Ministry of Education warned 15 universities for making insufficient progress against their development targets, and removed funded programmes at two of them.
Saudi Arabia's presence in THE's Top 500 rose from one university to nine. Vision 2030 set a target of at least five universities in the global Top 200.
—On QS, three universities are already in the Top 200: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (63), King Saud University (107) and King Abdulaziz University (200).
—On THE, only King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (176) makes the Top 200.
The UAE's presence in the Top 500 rose from zero to six universities on THE and from three to six on QS, the second-largest gain in the Gulf after Saudi Arabia.
—On QS, only Khalifa University (147) makes the Top 200.
—On THE, no UAE university makes the Top 200; Khalifa University and United Arab Emirates University come closest, at a joint 235th rank.
The US is still the largest cohort in both rankings, but its university count in THE's Top 500 fell from 122 to 96 between 2016 and 2027.
—The decline was concentrated among public universities outside the Top 100. Harvard, MIT and Stanford have held their positions.
—The decline is partly relative, as universities in Asia have moved up the table, and the bar has risen with them: the score needed for 100th place on THE rose from 58.0 in 2016 to 66.6 in 2027, so a university that held its score would still have slipped. It is also partly real, as in recent THE rankings US universities have scored lower on the quality and impact of their research and on international students.

 

Interestingly, Singapore did not grow its presence in the Top 100.
Its THE count remained at two institutions, NUS and NTU, throughout the decade. Both, however, moved up the rankings.
■On THE, NUS rose from 24th to 15th and NTU from 54th to 28th.
■On QS, NUS climbed from 12th to 10th and NTU from 13th to 12th.

 

In the last decade, the number of universities participating in the rankings has grown.
■Between 2017 and 2027, the number of universities ranked increased by 1,317 on THE and by 588 on QS. Most of the new universities are ranked below the Top 500.
■However, some universities are withdrawing, often citing a lack of transparency in THE's methods. Between 2020 and 2026, 124 universities left THE's rankings, including seven Indian Institutes of Technology, Utrecht University and the University of Zurich.

 

The 2016 top universities barely changed: 17 of these 20 institutions are still in the Top 20 a decade later.
The real movement sits below this cohort, among institutions that weren't elite in 2016.
The biggest risers are linked to robust national funding programmes.
■Seven of the 15 biggest risers are mainland Chinese universities, all funded under the Double First-Class programme.
■Two more risers are Hong Kong universities (Hong Kong Polytechnic and the Chinese University of Hong Kong), funded by Hong Kong's University Grants Committee.
■Four are Korean universities funded by Brain Korea 21 (Yonsei, KAIST, Sungkyunkwan and Korea University), a graduate-research programme running since 1999.
■The other two are Germany's Charité, a specialist medical university funded by the Excellence Strategy, and Italy's University of Bologna.

 

The universities that climbed are the ones whose governments committed to sustained funding, paired with strong accountability mechanisms.

 

 

 
 
GCC SPOTLIGHT
 

 

The Gulf is part of the story

 

02
Over the past decade, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar have all grown their presence in the rankings. On THE, Saudi Arabia made the biggest gains, going from 1 university in the Top 500 to 9, while the UAE went from 0 to 6 and Qatar from 0 to 2. QS shows a similar pattern: Saudi Arabia and the UAE each doubled from 3 to 6, and Qatar rose from 1 to 2 universities.
United Arab Emirates

 

The UAE's approach has centred on building strong flagship universities, led by Khalifa University, alongside hosting campuses of leading foreign institutions. During the decade, its count in the THE Top 500 went from 0 to 6, and in the QS Top 500 from 3 to 6. After Khalifa, the UAE's strongest universities are United Arab Emirates University (UAEU; QS 217, THE 235) and the American University of Sharjah (QS 258).
■Khalifa University is the UAE's biggest riser. Its QS rank moved from the 401-410 band in 2017 to 147 in 2027, second in the Gulf only to Qatar University (393rd to 109th). On THE, it moved from the 501-600 band to 235 (joint rank with UAEU).
—The climb followed a 2017 merger with the Petroleum Institute and the Masdar Institute, creating a single flagship.
—The university attributes its rise to strategic investment in research, talent and global partnerships, and its hiring reflects this: it ranks 12th in the world on QS's international faculty measure.

 

■United Arab Emirates University and the American University of Sharjah are also climbing on QS. UAEU has risen 79 places in five years and now leads UAE universities on academic reputation and international research network. AUS reached its highest-ever position in 2027 and rose 112 places on graduate employment outcomes.
■Four of Abu Dhabi's government-backed universities do not appear in either ranking as UAE entries.
—NYUAD, IITAD and Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi are satellite campuses, ranked under New York University (QS 58, THE 29), IIT Delhi (QS 118; not in THE's table) and Sorbonne University (QS 73; withdrew from THE from the 2027 edition).
—MBZUAI is in neither table: both require undergraduate teaching, and its first undergraduates only arrived in 2025.

 

 

Saudi Arabia

 

Saudi Arabia spread its funding across a broad base of public universities. Its THE WUR Top 500 count went from 1 to 9, and its QS count from 3 to 6. Under Vision 2030, it set a target of at least five Saudi universities in the global Top 200 by 2030; three have already reached the Top 200 on QS (KFUPM, King Saud University and King Abdulaziz University).
■King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM) leads the group at QS rank 63, the first Arab university to break into the QS Top 100. It has built more than 20 research centres, added 43 undergraduate concentrations and grown its postdoc base roughly tenfold since 2020.
■King Saud University has climbed 120 places on QS, from 227th in 2017 to 107th in 2027, with most of the gain coming since 2025. It stands out for international research collaboration (24th in the world) and for how well its graduates find work (31st).
■King Abdulaziz University is still in the QS Top 200, but it has slipped on both rankings since peaking in 2023.
—On QS, it fell from 106th in 2023 to 200th in 2027. On THE, it fell from 101st to the 401–450 band.
—Its 2023 peak had rested partly on incentivising international researchers to list it as a secondary affiliation, which inflated citations without adding research capacity. When THE cut the weight of citation impact in 2024, its rank fell sharply.

 

■KAUST doesn't appear in either ranking.
—It's graduate-only, and both systems require undergraduate teaching.
—Instead, it has topped THE's Arab University Rankings in the 2024 to 2026 editions, while KFUPM leads QS's equivalent regional table.

 

 

Qatar

 

Qatar's education strategy was investing in branch campuses. Education City hosts Georgetown, Northwestern, Weill Cornell Medicine, Texas A&M, Carnegie Mellon, Virginia Commonwealth University and HEC Paris, all ranked under their home institutions. Qatar is now also building homegrown universities.
■Hamad Bin Khalifa University (HBKU) is now the Gulf's highest-ranked university on THE. It debuted in 2027 at 126 (QS 213), ahead of every Saudi and UAE university in the THE rankings.
■Qatar University has made the largest QS climb of any Gulf university. It rose from 393rd in 2017 to 109th in 2027 (THE 222), making it the country's top-ranked university on QS.

 

 

 
 
LEARNINGS & IMPLICATIONS
 

 

Rankings reward clear strategy from funders

 

03

01

Rankings reward a narrow set of outcomes

Rankings reward research output, internationalisation and reputation. They don't measure social mobility, regional impact or alignment with national priorities. Funding a university to climb the rankings means funding what rankings measure, not its overall quality and impact.

 

02

Know which ranking you're measured against

QS and THE often disagree, and both also publish regional and specialist rankings, each with its own rules and winners. KAUST, for instance, is excluded from both flagship rankings, yet it has topped THE's Arab University Rankings three years running.

 

03

A numbered, time-bound target works

Saudi Arabia set a target of at least five universities in the global Top 200 by 2030. It focused ministerial effort and created accountability, and it is delivering: three Saudi universities are now in the QS Top 200, and KFUPM became the first Arab university in the QS Top 100.

 

04

Funding an existing university pays off faster than building one

A new university takes more time to show results: KAUST (founded 2009) and MBZUAI (2019) still don't appear in the flagship rankings. Funding an existing one shows results faster: China's Double First-Class universities and Khalifa University climbed rankings significantly within five to seven years.

 

05

Branch campuses pay off through local collaborations

A branch campus is ranked under its home university, not the host country. Its value comes through collaboration: its researchers co-author with local universities, lifting their research output and international-network scores.

 

06

AI brings both upside and integrity risk

AI is starting to produce research itself: in September 2026, OpenAI announced that an AI system had produced a machine-verified proof on the Navier-Stokes equations. But the same tools also make it cheaper to produce low-quality papers and inflate citation counts. Universities with strong research-integrity and data systems are best placed to capture the upside.
